balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

nim.title: Net interest margin
nim.content:
NIM is net interest income as a percentage of interest-earning assets.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the core profitability metric of a lender; a few basis points move earnings materially.

What to watch:

  • NIM trend with the rate cycle
  • Funding cost versus lending yield

capitalReturns.title: CET1 ratio and ROTCE
capitalReturns.content:
CET1 ratio is Common Equity Tier 1 capital over risk-weighted assets -- the regulator's core solvency buffer. ROTCE (return on tangible common equity) is net income available to common shareholders over average tangible common equity -- the return the bank earns on the capital it is required to hold.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: management has guided ROTCE to 16-18% by the end of FY2027, up from ~15.1% in Q3 2026; a rising ROTCE at a stable-to-falling CET1 ratio means the bank is earning more per dollar of required capital, which funds the buyback (authorization raised to $1.95bn in Q3 2026) without diluting the capital base.

What to watch:

  • ROTCE closing the gap to the 16-18% target
  • CET1 ratio drifting toward the regulatory minimum as buybacks accelerate

efficiencyRatio.title: Efficiency ratio
efficiencyRatio.content:
Efficiency ratio is non-interest expense over total revenue (net interest income plus fee income) -- the cost of producing a dollar of revenue. Lower is better.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: management's TOP (Tapping Our Potential) cost program and the mix shift toward higher-margin, capital-light fee businesses (wealth, capital markets) are both aimed at bringing this ratio down to fund the ROTCE target.

What to watch:

  • Efficiency ratio improving even as fee income grows (not just expense cuts)
  • Spikes from one-off restructuring or technology spend

creditQuality.title: Net charge-off ratio and allowance coverage
creditQuality.content:
Net charge-off ratio is annualized loan losses actually written off over average loans. Allowance coverage ratio is the reserve held against the loan book over total loans -- how much of a future loss the bank has already provisioned for.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: net charge-offs fell ~15% QoQ and provisioning dropped ~19% QoQ in Q3 2026, the clearest sign so far that the planned run-off of office and other stressed commercial real estate exposure is working through the book rather than deteriorating further.

What to watch:

  • Net charge-off ratio rising while allowance coverage falls (reserves not keeping pace with losses)
  • Commercial real estate concentration versus the rest of the loan book

depositsLoans.title: Total deposits and total loans
depositsLoans.content:
Total deposits fund the balance sheet; total loans are the earning-asset side. The gap between them, invested in securities and short-term instruments, is the bank's liquidity cushion.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the stated strategy is gathering low-cost, "high-quality" deposits while loan growth stays disciplined -- Private Bank deposits and loans have been the primary growth engine, while legacy commercial real estate is intentionally running off.

What to watch:

  • Deposit growth outpacing loan growth (cheaper funding, more capacity to lend selectively)
  • Loan mix shifting toward Private Bank / Consumer and away from runoff CRE

niiMix.title: Net interest income vs non-interest income
niiMix.content:
Net interest income is the spread earned on loans and securities less funding cost; non-interest income is fee revenue from capital markets, wealth management, mortgage banking and payments.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: net interest income is still roughly 70% of revenue, but management is deliberately growing the fee lines (record wealth management fees of $109m in Q3 2026) to diversify away from rate-cycle dependence and lift ROTCE.

What to watch:

  • Fee income share of revenue rising over time
  • Net interest income tracking the NIM and earning-asset trend above, not diverging from it

tbvps.title: Tangible book value per share
tbvps.content:
Tangible book value per share is tangible common equity (equity less goodwill and intangibles) divided by shares outstanding -- the per-share liquidation-style floor value, excluding the premium paid for past acquisitions.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: steady TBVPS growth alongside the dividend increases and expanded buyback authorization is the clearest sign capital is being returned from genuine earnings growth, not just accounting adjustments.

What to watch:

  • TBVPS growth rate versus retained-earnings growth (buybacks below TBVPS are accretive, above it are dilutive to TBVPS)
  • AOCI (available-for-sale securities marks) swings distorting the trend

segmentRevenue.title: Segment revenue: Commercial vs Consumer Banking
segmentRevenue.content:
Citizens reports two primary operating segments: Commercial Banking (corporate and middle-market lending, capital markets) and Consumer Banking (retail, Private Bank, wealth, mortgage).

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the Private Bank and wealth build-out sits inside Consumer Banking and is the segment management points to for capital-light, fee-driven growth; Commercial Banking's growth is constrained by the planned CRE runoff.

What to watch:

  • Consumer Banking revenue growing faster than Commercial as the mix shift plays out
  • Either segment's revenue decoupling from its net income (cost allocation changes)

segmentNetIncome.title: Segment net income: Commercial vs Consumer Banking
segmentNetIncome.content:
Net income earned by each of Citizens' two reporting segments, before corporate/other eliminations.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: Consumer Banking's net income has been rising on Private Bank deposit and loan growth plus record wealth fees, while Commercial Banking's net income is held back by continued CRE-related provisioning even as charge-offs improve.

What to watch:

  • Which segment is driving the ROTCE improvement above
  • Commercial Banking net income stabilizing as CRE runoff completes

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For Citizens Financial Group, Inc.: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
